Controls drawn into pictures over buttons, a file input, a treegrid, switches and ranges

Five more controls from ui-feed.dev, rebuilt with HTML-in-canvas. In each one the control is part of a picture: waypoints on a hand-drawn map, a drop zone on a scrapbook page, a night's backup on a green screen, the switches on a kitchen worktop and a crop box on a cutting mat. I wanted to know how much of each picture the canvas could paint itself, with the native elements only where something is pressed, typed or read out.

Credit: every control on this page is a rebuild of a demo on ui-feed.dev, and each section links to the original it came from. The originals are far higher fidelity than these, so go and look at them. These are examples of what HTML-in-canvas makes possible with a native element underneath, not replacements. I worked from the published demos rather than their source: I looked at what each one does, worked out the mechanism and built it again. The designs and the ideas are theirs. The photos and the still life here are painted by the canvas, so no picture is borrowed.

Coast path

The map is painted once by the canvas: the squared paper, the cliffs in hatching, the contours and the path. Each waypoint is a <button> drawn as a ring, and one role="tooltip" card is filled in for the one you point at or move to with Tab. The card springs out of its waypoint on a stem. A tap pins it, a second tap or Escape lets it go.

Travel journal

A page of a scrapbook. The heading is cut out a letter at a time, the photos are a list, and the drop zone is a <label> round an <input type="file"> that covers it, so a click opens the file picker and a file dropped on it goes straight into the input. Each photo you add is tossed onto the page: it falls in turning and lands on a strip of tape. The form sends the files.

Photo backup

A <table role="treegrid"> of the night's jobs, with a row for each and a level for its place in the tree. The keys are a treegrid's: Up and Down, Right to open or go in, Left to close or go out. The canvas draws the time axis and a bar for each job, and draws each row as a slice of the table at a place that follows its row on a spring, so when a job closes the rows under it slide up. The line at the bottom is an <output> for the chosen job.

Hob child lock

Two <input type="checkbox" role="switch">s on the worktop. The hob's keys above them are in a <fieldset>, and the lock sets disabled on it, so every key goes dead at once and the canvas draws them dim. The lock key is outside the fieldset: hold it, or hold Space on it, for three seconds and the lock comes off, with a ring drawn round it as it counts. The description under the big switch changes with it.

Cutting mat

A crop box over a picture the canvas paints. Four <input type="range">s hold the left, top, width and height, and each one's limits follow the others so the box can't leave the picture. One empty <div> over the picture takes every drag, and where the drag starts says whether it moves an edge, a corner or the whole box. With a range focused, the arrow keys move its edge, which the canvas draws yellow. The size is an <output> on a yellow tag, in inches.

How it works

Each control is a custom element on the same base class as the scroll controls. Its shadow root holds a canvas with content="drawable", and the native elements are children of that canvas.

Most of each picture is painted by the canvas, once, into a plain canvas that is kept and drawn every frame. The native elements are drawn where something is pressed or read: a ring over a button, a card that is a tooltip, a drop zone that is a file input, a row of a table. An element that only takes input (the crop area, the waypoints) is drawn with no alpha, which puts its hit region where it is wanted and nothing on the screen.

Two of the controls draw one element in several pieces: the photos are slices of one list, and the backup rows are slices of one table. Each slice is turned or moved on its own, which is how a photo lands at a tilt and a row slides up.

Live checks

Findings

  • Most of each picture is painted once by the canvas and kept, and the native elements are drawn only where something is pressed or read. At rest none of the five raised a paint event in 500 ms.
  • An <input type="file"> stretched over a drawn drop zone took the click and the files, and the form sent them through ElementInternals as a FormData. Files were put in with a DataTransfer in the check; a real drag and drop onto a drawn input wasn't tried.
  • One element can be drawn as several pieces that move on their own: the photos are slices of one list, turned and dropped onto the page, and the rows of the backup are slices of one table on springs. The hit region is put back on the table once the rows stop.
  • A disabled fieldset turned every key of the hob off at once, including the radios for the zones, and the canvas only had to read fieldset.disabled to draw them dim.
  • A tooltip card is an ordinary element with role="tooltip" that every waypoint names in aria-describedby. It is drawn scaled out of its waypoint, so it isn't in the top layer and the canvas can draw it.
  • The test browser had none of the hand, display or terminal fonts of the originals, so the map and the scrapbook are in fallbacks. Taps, holds and drags worked on an emulated Pixel 7; nothing here has been run on a real phone.
